intro: At B2 you learnt to correct a detail with one strong word and to present in clear chunks. Now you take it further: widen your pitch range so your key words stand out, pause on purpose so your main point lands, and move the stress in long sentences to change what you mean. The recordings are read in one calm, natural voice, so the high words (CAPITALS) and pauses (|) are marked in the text: say every example out loud and exaggerate a little.
teachingNotes: Builds on b1-pron-rhythm-intonation (content words strong, arrows ↗ ↘ →, a wide range for surprise, flat = bored), b2-pron-connected-speech (elision, weak forms, gonna/wanna/gotta) and b2-pron-intonation-attitude (fall-rise for doubt, gentle rise for polite requests, contrastive stress 'I said TUESday, not THURSday', the five-way 'I didn't say she stole it', chunking with |: pause after an opening phrase or a long subject and before but/because; never inside the | report or ten | percent). Recap in a line; don't re-teach. New here: pitch range (step up on new information and on both sides of a contrast, keep old information low, fall at the end of a point, start a new point higher), thought groups in LONG sentences (a whole noun phrase is one unit; not after every word), pausing for effect, and meaning-changing stress in long sentences (the seven-way drill incl. DIDN'T and THE; everything after the stressed word stays low). Notation: CAPITALS = the high, stressed word; | = pause; ↘ = fall.

Pitch range = how far the voice travels between its low and high notes. Confident English speakers step up high on the key word of each chunk, make it a little longer and louder, keep the small words around it low and quick, and fall low ↘ at the end of a point ('finished, and sure'). What steps up: new information (She's from BAli); both sides of a contrast (Sales ROSE in JAKARTA but FELL in SURABAYA). What stays low: old information, even a noun at the end ('Did you like the hotel?' 'I LOVED the hotel.'): explain that this seems to break the 'last content word is strongest' rule because that rule is for new words. Node common error: every word at the same pitch and volume (flat delivery). Indonesian trap: Indonesian is usually spoken in a narrower, flatter range and carries emphasis with words (-lah, kok, memang, sangat); in an English presentation a flat range sounds bored or unsure and hides the key point. Many learners fear a wide range sounds 'lebay': what feels exaggerated to them usually sounds lively to English ears. Also avoid ending every statement level or rising (sounds unsure, as if asking permission).

Pausing: a thought group is a group of words that form one idea, said together, with a short pause after it. In long sentences the key unit is the noun phrase (a noun with all the words that describe it): 'a significant increase in sales' is one group. Node common error: 'a significant | increase in sales'; right: 'a significant increase in sales | over the last year'. Good boundaries: after a long subject, before a time or place phrase at the end, before but/because/although, after an opening phrase. Also wrong: pausing after every word when reading carefully (robotic); aim for chunks of about 3–8 words. Pause for effect = a chosen, slightly longer pause (about a second), once or twice per talk: BEFORE a key number or idea (And the result? | FORty percent more customers; ...was | LESS than fifty million rupiah) or AFTER a key point to let it sink in, or after a question to the audience. Explain why a pause after was/is seems to break the 'don't split groups' rule: it works only because it is clearly on purpose and followed by a strong, high key word; the key phrase itself stays together (fifty | million ✗). Overused, it sounds theatrical. Silence, not 'eee…/umm/apa ya': a silent pause sounds confident. Chunking often has more than one good answer: test only clear cases (a split noun phrase, a split number, or a pause explicitly placed right before the key result).

Meaning-changing stress: the stressed word is the part being corrected; everything else stays true, and everything AFTER it stays low and quick (if the last word is also stressed as usual, or every word is equal, the contrast disappears: node common error). Seven-way drill 'I didn't say he took the money': I = someone else said it; DIDN'T = a firm denial; SAY = I only hinted at it; HE = someone else took it; TOOK = he didn't take it (for example someone gave it to him); THE (said 'thee') = not that specific money, other money; MONEY = he took something else. THE is rare: recognise it, don't test it. Long work sentences work the same way: 'I didn't say we should close the Bandung office next year' (WE = our partner should; CLOSE = do something else with it, e.g. move it; BANDUNG = a different office). Contrastive stress recap: I said TUESday, not THURSday. Indonesian trap: Indonesian marks this with words (Bukan saya yang bilang…, …dia yang ambil, kantor yang di Bandung); translated word for word but said flat in English, the correction is lost.

Audio limits: every recording is read once by one natural TTS voice. It does NOT demonstrate a wide pitch range on demand, contrastive stress, effect pauses or exact pauses, and capitals or | in read-aloud text are not reliably voiced. So read-aloud English (tiles, examples, listen) is written in normal spelling without capitals or | marks; the glosses and notes carry the markings. Listening questions only test what comes from the words (what the speaker got wrong, so which word you raise in your correction); stress, pitch and pauses are tested in text with CAPITALS and |. If the learner asks to hear the difference, describe it (lift your hand on the key word, drop it at the end) and ask them to say it aloud, record it and exaggerate.

Scope: A0–B2 grammar (all tenses, conditionals, passives, relative clauses, reported speech). Keep C1 structures out of examples: no cleft sentences ('It was Sari who…', 'What we need is…'), no inversion, no subjunctive. Don't teach tone-unit theory (tonic syllable, nucleus, key and termination), uptalk as a dialect feature, or regional melodies; British and American speakers share these basic patterns. At C1 many prosody choices are style: say so, and keep tested answers to clear cases.

keyPoints.title: Widen your pitch range: step up on key words
keyPoints.explanation: Let your voice travel. Step up high on the key word of each chunk (new information, or both sides of a contrast), make it a little longer, keep old information and small words low, and fall ↘ at the end of a point. A narrow, flat range, with every word at the same pitch, sounds bored or unsure.

examples.en: Sales rose in Jakarta but fell in Surabaya.
examples.id: Penjualan naik di Jakarta tapi turun di Surabaya. (ROSE in JAKARTA | but FELL in SURABAYA ↘)

examples.en: Did you like the hotel? I loved the hotel.
examples.id: Kamu suka hotelnya? Aku suka banget hotelnya. (I LOVED the hotel: hotel sudah disebut, jadi tetap rendah)

id.title: Perlebar rentang nada: naik di kata kunci
id.explanation: Biarkan suaramu bergerak. Naikkan nada tinggi-tinggi di kata kunci setiap potongan (informasi baru, atau kedua sisi kontras), ucapkan sedikit lebih panjang, biarkan informasi lama dan kata-kata kecil tetap rendah, dan turunkan ↘ di akhir satu poin. Rentang nada yang sempit dan datar, semua kata di nada yang sama, terdengar bosan atau tidak yakin.

keyPoints.title: Pause between thought groups, and sometimes for effect
keyPoints.explanation: Keep each thought group together, especially a whole noun phrase: a significant increase in sales | over the last year (not a significant | increase). Don't pause after every word. A pause for effect is one you choose: a little longer, just before your key number or idea, or just after it to let it sink in. Use it rarely, and use silence, not 'eee…'.

examples.en: We saw a significant increase in sales over the last year.
examples.id: Kami melihat peningkatan penjualan yang signifikan selama setahun terakhir. (…a significant increase in sales | over the last year)

examples.en: And the result? Forty percent more customers.
examples.id: Dan hasilnya? Pelanggan bertambah empat puluh persen. (And the result? | FORty percent more customers ↘)

id.title: Beri jeda di antara kelompok kata, dan kadang untuk efek
id.explanation: Jaga setiap kelompok kata tetap utuh, terutama satu frasa kata benda: a significant increase in sales | over the last year (bukan a significant | increase). Jangan berhenti setelah setiap kata. Jeda untuk efek adalah jeda yang kamu pilih: sedikit lebih panjang, tepat sebelum angka atau ide kuncimu, atau tepat setelahnya supaya meresap. Pakai jarang-jarang, dan pakai diam, bukan 'eee…'.

keyPoints.title: Move the stress to change the meaning
keyPoints.explanation: In a long sentence, the stressed word is the part you're correcting, and everything after it stays low and quick. I didn't say HE took the money = someone else took it; I didn't SAY he took the money = I only hinted at it; I DIDN'T say he took the money = a firm denial. If every word is equal, the contrast is lost.

examples.en: I didn't say he took the money. His partner took it.
examples.id: Aku nggak bilang dia yang mengambil uangnya. Rekannya yang mengambil. (tekan HE)

examples.en: I didn't say we should close the Bandung office next year.
examples.id: Aku nggak bilang kita harus menutup kantor Bandung tahun depan. (tekan BANDUNG = kantor yang lain)

id.title: Pindahkan tekanan untuk mengubah makna
id.explanation: Dalam kalimat panjang, kata yang ditekan adalah bagian yang kamu koreksi, dan semua kata setelahnya tetap rendah dan cepat. I didn't say HE took the money = orang lain yang mengambil; I didn't SAY he took the money = aku cuma menyindir; I DIDN'T say he took the money = bantahan tegas. Kalau semua kata sama kuatnya, kontrasnya hilang.

guidedPractice.prompt: Budi asks: 'Is the client meeting in room four?' It's in room five. You answer: 'No, it's in room five.' Which word do you raise highest? Write it.
guidedPractice.hint: Only the room number is wrong, so only the new number steps up: No, it's in room FIVE.

guidedPractice.prompt: You finish an important point in your pitch: 'That's why we need a bigger budget.' To sound sure and finished, does your voice rise, stay level or fall at the end? Write one word.
guidedPractice.hint: The end of a point falls low ↘: 'finished, and I'm sure'.

guidedPractice.prompt: Dimas reads: 'We expect a steady | growth in exports over the next decade.' The pause splits a noun phrase. Where should his one pause go instead? Write the word he pauses after.
guidedPractice.hint: a steady growth in exports is one group; over the next decade is a time phrase at the end.

guidedPractice.prompt: Sari wants one pause for effect, just before her key idea: 'The biggest risk for our startup is time.' After which word does she pause?
guidedPractice.hint: Build up to the key word, then let it land high: …is | TIME.

guidedPractice.prompt: In 'I didn't say he took the money', which word do you stress so it means 'I only hinted at it'? Write it.
guidedPractice.hint: The part being corrected is how you said it: not said, only hinted. I didn't SAY…

independentPractice.prompt: Rina asks: 'So you think the Bandung team lost the files?' You think the Surabaya team lost them. In your answer 'I didn't say the Bandung team lost the files', which word do you stress? Write it.
independentPractice.hint: The team is the part you're correcting, so BANDUNG is strong and everything after it stays low.

independentPractice.prompt: Split this slide sentence into three thought groups with |: 'In the first quarter our team in Makassar signed four new contracts.'
expected: in the first quarter | our team in makassar | signed four new contracts
independentPractice.hint: Opening time phrase | long subject | the rest. Keep our team in Makassar and four new contracts together.

assessment.prompt: Pak Hasan asks Sari: 'Did you read the report from the Medan office?' Sari answers: 'I wrote the report from the Medan office.' Which one word should she raise highest? Write the word.
assessment.rubric: Correct: wrote (the new information and the contrast with read: I WROTE the report from the Medan office; the report from the Medan office was just mentioned, so it stays low). 'report', 'medan' or 'office' = 0 (old information: raising it would suggest a different report or office). 'i' = 20 (it would contrast Sari with another person, which isn't the point here).

assessment.prompt: Listen to Bu Ani's question. In fact, the budget went down by eight percent. You answer: 'No, it went down by eight percent.' Which one word do you raise highest? Write it.
assessment.listen: So the budget for the Makassar office went up by eight percent this year?
assessment.rubric: Correct: down (she said up; eight percent is right, so it stays low: No, it went DOWN by eight percent ↘). 'eight' or 'percent' = 0 (the number was right; raising it suggests a different number). 'went' = 20 (the verb isn't the part that's wrong). 'up' = 0 (that's her mistake, not your correction).

assessment.prompt: Rina rehearses this sentence with one pause: 'We saw a dramatic | reduction in delivery times over the past six months.' The pause splits a group that belongs together. Where should her one pause go instead? Write the word she pauses after.
assessment.rubric: Correct: times (a dramatic reduction in delivery times is one noun phrase; over the past six months is a time phrase at the end: …in delivery times | over the past six months). 'saw' = 20 (We saw is too short to be a thought group of its own). 'dramatic', 'reduction', 'delivery', 'past' or 'six' = 0 (they split a group).

assessment.prompt: Pak Hasan ends his talk with this sentence and wants one pause for effect, just before the surprising result: 'The number of customer complaints this month was zero.' After which word does he pause? Write the word.
assessment.rubric: Correct: was (The number of customer complaints this month was | ZERO: the listeners wait, then the key word lands high). 'month' = 40 (a natural pause after the long subject, but it doesn't come just before the key word zero). 'number', 'customer' or 'complaints' = 0 (they split a group).

assessment.prompt: Bu Ani says: 'I didn't say the Jakarta team should finish the report by Friday.' She means that a different team should finish it by Friday. Which one word does she stress? Write it.
assessment.rubric: Correct: Jakarta (the team is the part being corrected; everything after it stays low: I didn't say the JAKARTA team should finish the report by Friday). 'team' = 50 (right area, but the word that tells the teams apart is Jakarta). 'friday' = 0 (that would mean a different deadline). 'report' = 0 (a different document). 'i' = 0 (someone else said it).

assessment.prompt: Pak Hasan says: 'I didn't say Dimas should LEAD the new project.' (LEAD has extra stress.) What does he mean? Write A, B or C. A: Someone else should lead the new project. B: Dimas should have another role in the new project, for example support it. C: Dimas should lead a different project.
assessment.rubric: Correct: B (the stressed word is the part being corrected: not lead, but another role). A = 0 (that needs extra stress on DIMAS). C = 0 (that needs extra stress on NEW or PROJECT).

assessment.prompt: In a meeting, a colleague says to Sari: 'You told the client the deadline was impossible!' Sari never said that, and she wants to deny it firmly. In her answer 'I didn't say the deadline was impossible', which word does she stress? Write it.
assessment.rubric: Correct: didn't (a firm denial that contradicts the colleague: I DIDN'T say the deadline was impossible). 'i' = 40 (it denies that she said it, but suggests someone else did, shifting the blame). 'say' = 20 (it would mean she only hinted at it, which admits part of it). 'impossible' or 'deadline' = 0 (that would mean she said something else about it).

material.title: Pitch range: let your voice travel

blocks.text:
**Quick recap (B2):** you correct a detail with one strong word (*I said TUESday, not THURSday*) and you present in chunks with short pauses (*Last year | our sales | rose by ten percent*). Now we go further.

**Pitch range** (rentang nada) = how far your voice travels between its lowest and highest notes. Confident English speakers use a **wide** range: the voice **steps up** high on the key word of each chunk, that word is a little **longer and louder**, and the small words around it stay low and quick. At the end of a point the voice **falls** low ↘: it says 'I've finished, and I'm sure.'

**What steps up?**
- **New information**, the word that tells the listener something new: *We've hired a new designer. She's from BAli.*
- **Both sides of a contrast**: *Sales ROSE in JAKARTA | but FELL in SURABAYA.*

**What stays low? Old information.** A word that was just mentioned stays low, even a noun at the end: *'Did you like the hotel?' 'I LOVED the hotel.'* This seems to break the rule from B1 and B2 that the **last** content word is the strongest. The reason: that rule is for **new** words. *Hotel* is old (it was in the question), so the peak moves to the new part, *loved*.

**Start each new point a little higher** (a new slide, a new topic) and let it fall at the end.

**The Indonesian trap:** Indonesian is usually spoken in a **narrower, flatter** range, and emphasis is often carried by words (*-lah, kok, memang, sangat*). Carried into English, a narrow range makes every word equal: in a presentation you sound **bored** or **unsure**, and listeners can't find your key point. Many learners also worry that a wide range sounds 'lebay'. To English ears, a range that feels exaggerated to you usually sounds simply lively and confident.

Avoid the opposite habit too: if every statement ends level or going up ↗, you sound as if you're asking permission or doubt your own data.

id.text:
**Ulasan singkat (B2):** kamu mengoreksi satu detail dengan satu kata yang kuat (*I said TUESday, not THURSday*) dan presentasi dalam potongan-potongan dengan jeda singkat (*Last year | our sales | rose by ten percent*). Sekarang kita lanjut.

**Rentang nada** (pitch range) = seberapa jauh suaramu bergerak antara nada terendah dan tertingginya. Penutur bahasa Inggris yang percaya diri memakai rentang yang **lebar**: suaranya **naik** tinggi di kata kunci setiap potongan, kata itu sedikit **lebih panjang dan lebih keras**, dan kata-kata kecil di sekitarnya tetap rendah dan cepat. Di akhir satu poin, suaranya **turun** rendah ↘: artinya 'sudah selesai, dan aku yakin.'

**Apa yang dinaikkan?**
- **Informasi baru**, kata yang memberi tahu pendengar sesuatu yang baru: *We've hired a new designer. She's from BAli.*
- **Kedua sisi kontras** (perbandingan): *Sales ROSE in JAKARTA | but FELL in SURABAYA.*

**Apa yang tetap rendah? Informasi lama.** Kata yang baru saja disebut tetap rendah, walaupun kata benda di akhir kalimat: *'Did you like the hotel?' 'I LOVED the hotel.'* Ini kelihatannya melanggar aturan dari B1 dan B2 bahwa kata isi yang **terakhir** paling kuat. Alasannya: aturan itu berlaku untuk kata yang **baru**. *Hotel* sudah lama (sudah ada di pertanyaan), jadi puncaknya pindah ke bagian yang baru, *loved*.

**Mulai setiap poin baru sedikit lebih tinggi** (slide baru, topik baru) dan biarkan turun di akhir.

**Jebakan untuk orang Indonesia:** bahasa Indonesia biasanya diucapkan dengan rentang nada yang **lebih sempit dan datar**, dan penekanan sering dibawa oleh kata (*-lah, kok, memang, sangat*). Kalau kebiasaan ini terbawa ke bahasa Inggris, semua kata jadi sama: saat presentasi kamu terdengar **bosan** atau **tidak yakin**, dan pendengar tidak menemukan poin utamamu. Banyak juga yang khawatir rentang yang lebar terdengar 'lebay'. Bagi telinga penutur bahasa Inggris, rentang yang terasa berlebihan bagimu biasanya terdengar hidup dan percaya diri saja.

Hindari juga kebiasaan sebaliknya: kalau setiap kalimat berakhir datar atau naik ↗, kamu terdengar seperti minta izin atau ragu pada datamu sendiri.

rows.en: This isn't a small problem. It's a serious one.
rows.id: Ini bukan masalah kecil. Ini masalah serius.

rows.id: Laba kami tumbuh tiga puluh persen.

blocks.text: Record one slide of your next presentation and listen back. Can you hear one clear high word in each group, and a fall at the end of each point? If everything sounds level, practise with your hand: lift it on the key word and drop it at the end.

id.text: Rekam satu slide dari presentasimu berikutnya dan dengarkan lagi. Apakah terdengar satu kata yang jelas tinggi di setiap kelompok, dan nada turun di akhir setiap poin? Kalau semuanya terdengar datar, latihan dengan tanganmu: angkat tangan di kata kunci dan turunkan di akhir.

blocks.prompt: Rina presents her startup to investors in a narrow, flat range: every word at the same pitch and volume, every sentence ending level. What is the most likely effect?
options: She sounds bored or unsure, and her key points get lost.
blocks.explain: A flat, narrow range makes every word equal, so listeners can't find the key points, and level endings sound unsure. Calm and professional comes from clear high key words and confident falls ↘, not from flatness. Too emotional is the opposite problem.

id.prompt: Rina mempresentasikan startup-nya kepada investor dengan rentang nada yang sempit dan datar: semua kata di nada dan volume yang sama, setiap kalimat berakhir datar. Apa efek yang paling mungkin?
id.explain: Rentang yang datar dan sempit membuat semua kata sama, jadi pendengar tidak menemukan poin kuncinya, dan akhir kalimat yang datar terdengar tidak yakin. Tenang dan profesional datang dari kata kunci yang jelas tinggi dan nada turun ↘ yang yakin, bukan dari kedataran. Terlalu emosional adalah masalah sebaliknya.
options: Terdengar bosan atau tidak yakin, dan poin pentingnya tenggelam.

blocks.text:
At B2 you chunked short slide sentences. At C1 your sentences are longer, with long **noun phrases** (a noun plus all the words that describe it), so the question is: where does one **thought group** (one idea said together) end?

**A whole noun phrase is one group.** *a significant increase in sales* is one idea: the noun (*increase*), the words before it (*a significant*) and the phrase after it (*in sales*). Don't pause inside it:
- ✗ *We saw a significant | increase in sales over the last year.*
- ✓ *We saw a significant increase in sales | over the last year.*

**Good places for a pause in a long sentence:**
- after a long subject: *The new rules for online sellers | come into force in May.*
- before a time or place phrase at the end: *| over the last year*, *| across Java*;
- before *but, because, although, which*;
- after an opening phrase: *In the second quarter |*.

**Not after every word, either.** When people read carefully in a foreign language they often stop between words: *We | saw | a | significant | increase…* It sounds robotic and slow, and the listener can't hear which words belong together. Aim for groups of about 3–8 words.

**The trap:** pausing where you run out of breath or stop to think of the next word, often right in the middle of a noun phrase. Note that Indonesian puts the describing words after the noun (*peningkatan penjualan yang signifikan*), while English puts them around it (*a significant increase in sales*): the whole block still goes together. Plan your groups before you speak, and breathe at the |.

Long sentences can often be chunked in more than one good way. What's never good: splitting a noun phrase, a number from its word (*ten | percent*), or a preposition from its noun (*in | Bandung*).

id.text:
Di B2 kamu memotong kalimat slide yang pendek. Di C1 kalimatmu lebih panjang, dengan **frasa kata benda** yang panjang (kata benda plus semua kata yang menjelaskannya), jadi pertanyaannya: di mana satu **kelompok kata** (thought group, satu ide yang diucapkan bersama) berakhir?

**Satu frasa kata benda utuh = satu kelompok.** *a significant increase in sales* adalah satu ide: kata bendanya (*increase*), kata sebelumnya (*a significant*) dan frasa sesudahnya (*in sales*). Jangan berhenti di dalamnya:
- ✗ *We saw a significant | increase in sales over the last year.*
- ✓ *We saw a significant increase in sales | over the last year.*

**Tempat yang baik untuk jeda dalam kalimat panjang:**
- setelah subjek yang panjang (subjek = siapa atau apa yang dibicarakan): *The new rules for online sellers | come into force in May.*
- sebelum keterangan waktu atau tempat di akhir: *| over the last year*, *| across Java*;
- sebelum *but, because, although, which*;
- setelah frasa pembuka: *In the second quarter |*.

**Jangan juga berhenti setelah setiap kata.** Saat membaca dengan hati-hati dalam bahasa asing, orang sering berhenti di antara kata: *We | saw | a | significant | increase…* Terdengar seperti robot dan lambat, dan pendengar tidak bisa mendengar kata mana yang satu kelompok. Usahakan kelompok sekitar 3–8 kata.

**Jebakannya:** berhenti saat kehabisan napas atau saat mencari kata berikutnya, sering tepat di tengah frasa kata benda. Perhatikan bahwa bahasa Indonesia menaruh kata penjelas setelah kata benda (*peningkatan penjualan yang signifikan*), sedangkan bahasa Inggris menaruhnya di sekitarnya (*a significant increase in sales*): seluruh blok itu tetap satu kelompok. Rencanakan kelompok katamu sebelum bicara, dan ambil napas di tanda |.

Kalimat panjang sering bisa dipotong dengan lebih dari satu cara yang baik. Yang tidak pernah baik: memecah frasa kata benda, memisahkan angka dari katanya (*ten | percent*), atau kata depan dari kata bendanya (*in | Bandung*).

rows.en: We saw a significant increase in sales over the last year.
rows.id: Kami melihat peningkatan penjualan yang signifikan selama setahun terakhir.
rows.note: We saw a significant increase in sales | over the last year (not a significant | increase)

id.note: We saw a significant increase in sales | over the last year (bukan a significant | increase)

rows.en: The new rules for online sellers come into force in May.
rows.id: Aturan baru untuk penjual online mulai berlaku bulan Mei.
rows.note: long subject: The new rules for online sellers | come into force in May

id.note: subjek panjang: The new rules for online sellers | come into force in May

rows.en: The survey of three hundred nurses in Surabaya showed a clear link between night shifts and poor sleep.

blocks.text: Before a talk, print your script and mark the | in pencil. Then read each group in one breath. If you need to breathe inside a group, the group is too long: find an earlier natural boundary.

id.text: Sebelum presentasi, cetak naskahmu dan tandai | dengan pensil. Lalu baca setiap kelompok dalam satu tarikan napas. Kalau kamu perlu bernapas di tengah kelompok, kelompoknya terlalu panjang: cari batas alami yang lebih awal.

blocks.prompt: Which version pauses in the wrong place?
options: The company plans to open a large new | warehouse near Semarang next year.
The company plans to open a large new warehouse near Semarang | next year.
The company plans to open | a large new warehouse near Semarang | next year.
blocks.explain: *a large new warehouse near Semarang* is one noun phrase, so a large new | warehouse splits it. Pausing before the time phrase *next year*, or after *plans to open*, keeps every group together.

id.prompt: Versi mana yang jedanya di tempat yang salah?
id.explain: *a large new warehouse near Semarang* adalah satu frasa kata benda, jadi a large new | warehouse memecahnya. Jeda sebelum keterangan waktu *next year*, atau setelah *plans to open*, menjaga setiap kelompok tetap utuh.

blocks.text:
A **pause for effect** is a pause you **choose**, not one you need. It's a little longer than a normal pause between groups (about one second), and you save it for your most important point:
- **Before** a key number or idea, to build suspense. The listeners wait, then the key word lands with a high step up: *And the result? | FORty percent more customers.* *We need one thing from this team: | SPEED.* *The total cost of the project was | LESS than fifty million rupiah.*
- **After** a key point, to let it sink in: *FORty percent. | That's the best result in our history.*
- **After a question** to the audience, so they really think: *What would you do with an extra hour a day? |*

**Doesn't 'was | less than fifty million' break the rule?** Normally you wouldn't pause between *was* and what follows it. It works here only because it's clearly **on purpose**: a little longer, used once, and followed by a strong, high key word. The key phrase itself stays together: *fifty | million* ✗, *less than | fifty million* ✗.

**Use it rarely.** One or two pauses for effect in a five-minute talk are plenty. After every sentence it sounds theatrical, like a TV quiz show host.

**Silence, not 'eee…'.** A filled pause (*eee…, umm…, apa ya…*) sounds unsure; the same length of **silence** sounds calm and confident. Many presenters fill every gap out of nerves: practise standing in silence for one second and looking at your audience.

id.text:
**Jeda untuk efek** adalah jeda yang kamu **pilih**, bukan yang kamu butuhkan. Sedikit lebih panjang dari jeda biasa antarkelompok kata (sekitar satu detik), dan kamu simpan untuk poin terpentingmu:
- **Sebelum** angka atau ide kunci, untuk membangun rasa penasaran. Pendengar menunggu, lalu kata kuncinya mendarat dengan nada naik yang tinggi: *And the result? | FORty percent more customers.* *We need one thing from this team: | SPEED.* *The total cost of the project was | LESS than fifty million rupiah.*
- **Setelah** poin kunci, supaya meresap: *FORty percent. | That's the best result in our history.*
- **Setelah pertanyaan** kepada audiens, supaya mereka benar-benar berpikir: *What would you do with an extra hour a day? |*

**Bukankah 'was | less than fifty million' melanggar aturan?** Biasanya kamu tidak berhenti di antara *was* dan kata sesudahnya. Di sini jeda itu berhasil hanya karena jelas **disengaja**: sedikit lebih panjang, dipakai sekali, dan diikuti kata kunci yang kuat dan tinggi. Frasa kuncinya sendiri tetap utuh: *fifty | million* ✗, *less than | fifty million* ✗.

**Pakai jarang-jarang.** Satu atau dua jeda untuk efek dalam presentasi lima menit sudah cukup. Kalau setelah setiap kalimat, terdengar teatrikal, seperti pembawa acara kuis di TV.

**Diam, bukan 'eee…'.** Jeda yang diisi (*eee…, umm…, apa ya…*) terdengar tidak yakin; **diam** dengan panjang yang sama terdengar tenang dan percaya diri. Banyak presenter mengisi setiap celah karena gugup: latih dirimu untuk diam satu detik sambil menatap audiens.

blocks.prompt: Sari wants one pause for effect, to build suspense before her key figure: 'This year, the number of active users reached one million.' Where does it go?
options: This year, the number | of active users reached one million.
This year, the number of active users reached | one million.
This year, the number of active users reached one | million.
blocks.explain: The pause for effect comes just before the key figure, so the listeners wait and then *one MILlion* lands high. *the number | of active users* splits a noun phrase, and *one | million* splits the number itself.

id.prompt: Sari ingin satu jeda untuk efek, untuk membangun rasa penasaran sebelum angka kuncinya: 'This year, the number of active users reached one million.' Di mana jedanya?
id.explain: Jeda untuk efek datang tepat sebelum angka kunci, jadi pendengar menunggu lalu *one MILlion* mendarat tinggi. *the number | of active users* memecah frasa kata benda, dan *one | million* memecah angkanya sendiri.

material.title: Move the stress, change the meaning

blocks.text:
**Recap (B2):** you moved the stress to correct one detail (*I said TUESday, not THURSday*) and saw that *I didn't say she stole it* changes meaning with the stressed word.

At C1 the sentences are longer, so there are more words to choose from, and one rule matters more: **after the stressed word, everything stays low and quick.** If you also stress the last word as usual, or say every word with equal stress, the listener hears no contrast at all, and your meaning is lost.

**The classic drill: one sentence, seven meanings.** *I didn't say he took the money.* The stressed word is the part you're correcting; everything else stays true (see the examples below). Two are new since B2:
- **DIDN'T** stressed = a **firm denial** that contradicts someone: 'You said he took it!' 'I DIDN'T say he took the money.'
- **THE** stressed, said 'thee' = *that specific* money, the money everyone is talking about: he took some money, just not that money. This one is rare: recognise it.

**In long work sentences it's the same:** *I didn't say we should close the Bandung office next year.*
- *WE* → someone else (our partner) should close it;
- *CLOSE* → we should do something else with it, for example move it;
- *BANDUNG* → we should close a different office.

**The Indonesian trap:** Indonesian usually shows this with words: *Bukan saya yang bilang…*, *Saya nggak bilang dia **yang** ambil…*, *…kantor **yang di Bandung***. If you translate the words but keep a flat English voice, the correction disappears. In English, the voice alone does the job.

id.text:
**Ulasan (B2):** kamu memindahkan tekanan untuk mengoreksi satu detail (*I said TUESday, not THURSday*) dan melihat bahwa *I didn't say she stole it* berubah arti sesuai kata yang ditekan.

Di C1 kalimatnya lebih panjang, jadi lebih banyak kata yang bisa dipilih, dan satu aturan jadi lebih penting: **setelah kata yang ditekan, semuanya tetap rendah dan cepat.** Kalau kamu juga menekan kata terakhir seperti biasa, atau mengucapkan semua kata sama kuatnya, pendengar tidak mendengar kontras sama sekali, dan maksudmu hilang.

**Latihan klasik: satu kalimat, tujuh arti.** *I didn't say he took the money.* Kata yang ditekan adalah bagian yang kamu koreksi; sisanya tetap benar (lihat contoh di bawah). Dua di antaranya baru sejak B2:
- **DIDN'T** ditekan = **bantahan tegas** yang membantah orang lain: 'You said he took it!' 'I DIDN'T say he took the money.'
- **THE** ditekan, dibaca 'thii' = uang *yang itu*, uang yang sedang dibicarakan semua orang: dia memang mengambil uang, tapi bukan uang yang itu. Ini jarang: cukup dikenali.

**Dalam kalimat kerja yang panjang sama saja:** *I didn't say we should close the Bandung office next year.*
- *WE* → orang lain (mitra kita) yang harus menutupnya;
- *CLOSE* → kita harus melakukan hal lain dengan kantor itu, misalnya memindahkannya;
- *BANDUNG* → kita harus menutup kantor yang lain.

**Jebakan untuk orang Indonesia:** bahasa Indonesia biasanya menunjukkan ini dengan kata: *Bukan saya yang bilang…*, *Saya nggak bilang dia **yang** ambil…*, *…kantor **yang di Bandung***. Kalau kamu menerjemahkan kata-katanya tapi suaramu tetap datar dalam bahasa Inggris, koreksinya hilang. Dalam bahasa Inggris, suara saja sudah cukup untuk melakukannya.

blocks.text: Practise the drill aloud, one meaning at a time, and say the follow-up sentence too. Then ask a friend to cover the follow-ups: can they guess the meaning from your stress alone?

id.text: Latih drill ini dengan suara keras, satu arti setiap kali, dan ucapkan juga kalimat lanjutannya. Lalu minta teman menutup kalimat lanjutannya: bisakah dia menebak artinya dari tekananmu saja?

blocks.prompt: Bu Ani says: 'I didn't say the client in Medan wanted a discount.' She means the client wanted something else, for example free delivery. Which word does she stress?
blocks.explain: The part being corrected is what the client wanted: not a *discount* but free delivery, so *DISCOUNT* is strong. *MEDAN* would mean a different client; *WANTED* would mean the client didn't want it, for example only asked about it.

id.prompt: Bu Ani bilang: 'I didn't say the client in Medan wanted a discount.' Maksudnya klien itu menginginkan hal lain, misalnya gratis ongkir. Kata mana yang dia tekan?
id.explain: Bagian yang dikoreksi adalah apa yang diinginkan klien: bukan *discount* tapi gratis ongkir, jadi *DISCOUNT* yang kuat. *MEDAN* berarti klien yang lain; *WANTED* berarti klien tidak menginginkannya, misalnya cuma menanyakannya.

material.title: Putting it together: a marked script

blocks.text:
Here's how a presenter might mark a short script: CAPITALS for the high, stressed words, | for pauses, ↘ where the voice falls at the end of a point, and || for one pause for effect.

*Good MORNing, everyone. ↘ | In the last QUARter | our team in BANdung | handled TWICE as many orders ↘ | with the SAME number of staff. ↘ | And the reason? || autoMAtion. ↘ | NOW | let's look at our COSTS.*

Notice: one high word per group; *orders* stays low in *TWICE as many orders* because the new information is *twice*; the effect pause comes only once, before the key idea; the new point (*NOW*) starts higher.

These are strong tendencies, not strict laws. Two good speakers may chunk the same sentence a little differently. What every good version shares: clear high key words, groups that are never split, falls at the end of points, and silence instead of *eee…*.

id.text:
Begini cara seorang presenter menandai naskah pendek: HURUF BESAR untuk kata yang tinggi dan ditekan, | untuk jeda, ↘ di tempat suara turun di akhir satu poin, dan || untuk satu jeda untuk efek.

*Good MORNing, everyone. ↘ | In the last QUARter | our team in BANdung | handled TWICE as many orders ↘ | with the SAME number of staff. ↘ | And the reason? || autoMAtion. ↘ | NOW | let's look at our COSTS.*

Perhatikan: satu kata tinggi per kelompok; *orders* tetap rendah dalam *TWICE as many orders* karena informasi barunya adalah *twice*; jeda untuk efek hanya sekali, sebelum ide kunci; poin baru (*NOW*) dimulai lebih tinggi.

Ini kecenderungan yang kuat, bukan hukum yang kaku. Dua pembicara yang bagus bisa memotong kalimat yang sama sedikit berbeda. Yang sama dari setiap versi yang bagus: kata kunci yang jelas tinggi, kelompok kata yang tidak pernah dipecah, nada turun di akhir poin, dan diam, bukan *eee…*.

blocks.text: Shadow a good speaker: play a short clip of a talk, pause it after each group, and repeat it with the same high words and pauses. Then do the same with your own marked script.

id.text: Lakukan shadowing pada pembicara yang bagus: putar potongan pendek sebuah presentasi, hentikan setelah setiap kelompok kata, dan ulangi dengan kata tinggi dan jeda yang sama. Lalu lakukan hal yang sama dengan naskahmu sendiri yang sudah ditandai.

id.intro: Di B2 kamu sudah belajar mengoreksi satu detail dengan satu kata yang kuat dan presentasi dalam potongan yang jelas. Sekarang kita lanjut: perlebar rentang nadamu supaya kata kuncimu menonjol, beri jeda dengan sengaja supaya poin utamamu mengena, dan pindahkan tekanan dalam kalimat panjang untuk mengubah maksudmu. Rekamannya dibaca oleh satu suara yang tenang dan alami, jadi kata yang tinggi (HURUF BESAR) dan jeda (|) ditandai di teks: ucapkan setiap contoh dengan suara keras dan sedikit dilebih-lebihkan.

assessment.psd-1: Pak Hasan bertanya kepada Sari: 'Did you read the report from the Medan office?' Sari menjawab: 'I wrote the report from the Medan office.' Satu kata mana yang sebaiknya dia ucapkan paling tinggi? Tulis katanya dalam bahasa Inggris.
assessment.psd-2: Dengarkan pertanyaan Bu Ani. Sebenarnya anggarannya turun delapan persen. Kamu menjawab: 'No, it went down by eight percent.' Satu kata mana yang kamu ucapkan paling tinggi? Tulis katanya dalam bahasa Inggris.
assessment.psd-3: Rina berlatih membaca kalimat ini dengan satu jeda: 'We saw a dramatic | reduction in delivery times over the past six months.' Jedanya memecah kelompok kata yang seharusnya utuh. Di mana seharusnya satu jedanya? Tulis kata yang diucapkan tepat sebelum jeda.
assessment.psd-4: Pak Hasan menutup presentasinya dengan kalimat ini dan ingin satu jeda untuk efek, tepat sebelum hasil yang mengejutkan: 'The number of customer complaints this month was zero.' Setelah kata apa dia memberi jeda? Tulis katanya dalam bahasa Inggris.
assessment.psd-5: Bu Ani bilang: 'I didn't say the Jakarta team should finish the report by Friday.' Maksudnya tim lain yang harus menyelesaikannya paling lambat hari Jumat. Satu kata mana yang dia tekan? Tulis katanya.
assessment.psd-6: Pak Hasan bilang: 'I didn't say Dimas should LEAD the new project.' (LEAD diucapkan dengan tekanan ekstra.) Apa maksudnya? Tulis A, B atau C. A: Someone else should lead the new project. B: Dimas should have another role in the new project, for example support it. C: Dimas should lead a different project.
assessment.psd-7: Di sebuah rapat, seorang rekan berkata kepada Sari: 'You told the client the deadline was impossible!' Sari tidak pernah bilang begitu, dan dia ingin membantahnya dengan tegas. Dalam jawabannya 'I didn't say the deadline was impossible', kata mana yang dia tekan? Tulis katanya dalam bahasa Inggris.
